summary: Defines MIB objects for managing the configuration, monitoring and control of Physical Units and Logical Units in an SNA environment, using SMIv2. It replaced RFC 1665. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC is a catalogue of counters and switches that an SNMP manager can read and change on an SNA node or logical unit. It comes in two halves for every resource: the Admin table holds what you want to happen, and the Oper table holds what is actually happening now.

subtitle: The managed objects that let SNMP watch over SNA nodes and logical units.

tldr.problem: An SNA network has nodes and logical units that an operator needs to create, activate, watch and deactivate, and there was no standard way to reach them with SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a MIB module with an Admin table for each kind of resource and an Oper table that mirrors it with the values actually in use, plus row creation through the RowStatus object and traps for state changes and failures.
tldr.outcome: The module covers PU types 1.0, 2.0 and 2.1 and LU types 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 7, with generic objects for LU 6.2. It obsoleted RFC 1665, and the RFC Editor index lists its status as Historic.

facts.label: LU types covered
facts.value: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 7, with generic objects also for 6.2

facts.label: Traps
facts.value: Node state change, node activation failure, LU state change, LU session BIND failure

today: RFC 1666 is an August 1994 standards-track memo, and the RFC Editor index lists its status as Historic. It obsoleted RFC 1665, and no later RFC obsoletes it, so it is kept here as a record of the SNA NAU management objects.

sections.title: What the MIB Manages
sections.content:
The memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base for use with network management protocols in the Internet community, and in particular defines objects for managing the configuration, monitoring and control of Physical Units and Logical Units in an SNA environment. Physical Units and Logical Units are two types of Network Addressable Unit in the logical structure of an SNA network, and NAUs are the origination or destination points for SNA data streams.

The memo identifies managed objects for PU type 1.0, 2.0 and type 2.1, and for LU type 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 7. The generic objects defined there can also be used to manage LU 6.2 and any LU-LU session. The SNA terms and the overall architecture are documented in the IBM Systems Network Architecture Technical Overview.

The SNMPv2 network management framework the module belongs to has four major components: the SMI, the mechanisms used for describing and naming objects for the purpose of management, which is RFC 1442; MIB-II, the core set of managed objects for the Internet suite of protocols, which is RFC 1213; the administrative and other architectural aspects of the framework, which is RFC 1445; and the protocol used for network access to managed objects, which is RFC 1448. The framework permits new objects to be defined for the purpose of experimentation and evaluation.

Managed objects are accessed through a virtual information store, the MIB. Objects are defined using the subset of ASN.1 defined in the SMI, and each object type is named by an object identifier, an administratively assigned name. The object type together with an object instance identifies a specific instantiation of the object, and for human convenience a textual string, the descriptor, is often used to refer to the object type.
sections.plainLanguage: SNA calls the machines on the network nodes and the endpoints of a conversation logical units. This RFC gives each of them a set of values that an SNMP manager can read, and some that it can write.

sections.title: The Structure of the MIB
sections.content:
The document uses the name Node for SNA node type 1.0, 2.0 and type 2.1, and the name LU for logical unit of type 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 7 and 6.2. Only objects common to all PU and LU types are covered, and LU 6.2 specific objects are not included in the module.

The SNANAU MIB module contains three groups of objects: snaNode, for objects related to node configuration, monitoring and control; snaLu, for objects related to LU definition, monitoring and control; and snaMgtTools, for objects related to specific management tools well known in an SNA environment. That last group is optional.

The objects related to PUs and LUs are organized into two kinds of table, the Admin and the Oper tables. The Admin table contains parameters used by a management station to affect the operation of the SNA service. Some of them are used to initialize and configure the service at the next startup, while others can take effect immediately. A management station can define SNA resources dynamically by creating new entries in the Admin table, and it uses a special object, AdminState, to control the desired state of a defined PU or LU session resource. The memo notes that this MIB does not allow the manipulation of an LU's operational state.

The Oper table is an extension, or augment, of the corresponding Admin table, and holds the objects that correspond to the values of parameters currently used by the SNA system. The module also uses the TimeStamp textual convention, defined as the value of the MIB II sysUpTime object when a specific occurrence happens, and the occurrences related to SNA NAU management are defined in the module itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything is in pairs of tables. The Admin table is what you want: a node you have created, switched on. The Oper table is what is: the node's actual running state, and the counters it keeps.

sections.title: The Node and Logical Unit Tables
sections.content:
The snaNode group consists of six tables and two traps. The snaNodeAdminTable contains objects that describe the configuration parameters of an SNA node, and its entries can be created, modified and deleted by either an agent or a management station, with the snaNodeAdminRowStatus object describing the status of an entry and used to change it. The snaNodeAdminState object describes the desired operational state of a node and is used to change it. Link-specific configuration objects live in a separate MIB module, such as the SNA DLC MIB module, that corresponds to the link type.

For each entry in the snaNodeAdminTable there is a corresponding entry in the snaNodeOperTable, which holds the runtime and operational state variables for the node and uses the same index. Its rows are created by an agent as soon as the Admin table entry becomes active, and they cannot be modified by a management station. The snaPu20StatsTable holds statistics counters for a PU 2.0, indexed by the node index, with rows created by the agent when the corresponding Admin table entry becomes active. The snaNodeLinkAdminTable holds all references to the link-specific tables, so a node with several links has several entries, and the snaNodeLinkOperTable is the operational counterpart of it. Two traps are defined for nodes: snaNodeStateChangeTrap, which indicates that the operational state of a node has changed, and snaNodeActFailTrap, which indicates the failure of an ACTPU received from the host.

The snaLu group has a similar shape. The snaLuAdminTable holds LU configuration information and its rows can be created and deleted by a management station, with only objects common to all types of LU included. The snaLuOperTable holds dynamic runtime information and control variables and augments it. The snaLuSessnTable describes the operational state of LU-LU sessions, with an entry created by the agent when a session appears and removed when the session's operational state changes to unbound. The snaLuSessnStatsTable holds dynamic statistics for those sessions and cannot be created by a management station. Two traps are defined for LUs: snaLuStateChangeTrap, which indicates that the operational state of an LU has changed, and snaLuSessnBindFailTrap, which indicates the failure of a BIND request.

The optional snaMgtTools group holds the snaLuRtmTable, whose rows hold Response Time Monitor variables for an LU, indexed by node and LU, corresponding to the LU 2 entries in the snaLuAdminTable, so that a management station can read a collection of response time statistics for a given LU.
sections.plainLanguage: For a node there are tables for its configuration, its running state, its counters, and its links. For a logical unit there are tables for its configuration, its running state, its sessions and the session counters. Four traps tell the manager when something changes or fails.

sections.title: Creating Rows and Changing State
sections.content:
The row creation mechanism for the Admin tables is based on the use of the RowStatus object, and restrictions on some operations for specific tables are described in each table. In particular, before accepting the destroy value for an entry, an agent has to verify the operational state of the corresponding entry in the Oper table.

The state diagram for nodes models the transitions between the operational states inactive, active, waiting and stopping, against the two values of the AdminState, active and inactive. When a row is created by a management station, the agent creates the Oper table entry for that node with the operational state set to inactive, and the agent cannot accept any operations for that node until the RowStatus is set to active. Setting the administrative state to active while the node is inactive starts the node's activation, and setting it to inactive while the node is active initiates the node shutdown process using the method indicated by snaNodeOperStopMethod, which may leave the node stopping or inactive. A node in the waiting state follows the active administration in the same way and returns to inactive when the administrative state is inactive, and a node in the stopping state cannot be activated while it is there.

The state diagram for sessions models the transitions between the states unbound, pendingBind, bound and pendingUnbind, again against the administrative states bound and unbound. When a session goes to the unbound state, the corresponding entry is removed from the session table by the agent.
sections.plainLanguage: To create a node, the manager writes a row and marks it active, and the agent then brings the node up. To delete one, the manager has to wait until the node is inactive, so that nothing is torn down while it is in use.

sections.title: Conformance
sections.content:
Compliance of an SNMPv2 management entity to the SNANAU MIB is defined in terms of conformance units called groups. The unconditionally mandatory groups are snaNodeGroup, snaLuGroup and snaSessionGroup. The conditionally mandatory groups are snaPu20Group, mandatory only for entities that implement PU type 2.0, and snaMgtToolsRtmGroup, mandatory only for entities that implement LU type 2 and RTM.

There is a refinement of the requirements for object access: an agent that does not implement row creation for snaNodeAdminTable, snaNodeLinkAdminTable and snaLuAdminTable must at least support object modification requests, that is, read-write access instead of read-create.

The module does not support the creation of links, the activation or deactivation of LUs, nor the activation of sessions. Among the management functions it does support are the creation and deletion of nodes and LUs through the RowStatus objects, the creation and deletion of the table entries associating node instances with link instances, the activation and deactivation of nodes through the AdminState object, the deactivation of sessions through the AdminState object in the session table, monitoring and modification of the parameters related to nodes, LUs and node and link associations, monitoring of session operational parameters, PU 2.0 operational statistics, session operational statistics, RTM statistics, and traps for node state change, node activation failure, LU state change and LU session BIND failure.
sections.plainLanguage: Every implementation must be able to manage nodes, logical units and sessions. The counters for PU 2.0 and the response time tool are only required if the device has the matching hardware.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says in one line that security issues are not discussed in it. The access rules in the module are the ones inherited from the SNMPv2 framework, and the module's own contribution is to make some of the objects read-create, which is what lets a management station create and delete SNA resources remotely.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says nothing about security. The manager that can create and switch on nodes here is a manager that should be trusted.
